blocks.text: A 58-year-old man wakes with a drooping right upper eyelid and a right eye that points down and out. His left arm and left leg are weak. Two apparently unrelated problems on opposite sides of the body point to one small lesion in a structure no wider than a thumb.

blocks.markdown: The **brainstem** connects the forebrain to the spinal cord and cerebellum. From rostral to caudal it comprises the **midbrain**, **pons** and **medulla oblongata**. It contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III to XII, the long ascending and descending tracts, and the **reticular formation**. A useful organising plan, at every level, divides the brainstem into a **tectum** (dorsal), a **tegmentum** (containing cranial nerve nuclei and the reticular formation) and a **basis** (ventral, carrying the descending corticospinal fibres).

**Midbrain.** Contains the superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculi (auditory relay) in the tectum, the substantia nigra and red nucleus, and the cerebral peduncles ventrally. **Cranial nerve III (oculomotor)** exits from the interpeduncular fossa on the ventral surface. **Cranial nerve IV (trochlear)** is unique: it exits **dorsally**, just below the inferior colliculus, and is the only cranial nerve to do so.

**Pons.** The bulging ventral pons contains pontine nuclei and corticospinal fibres in the basis. **CN V (trigeminal)** attaches laterally at mid-pons. At the **pontomedullary junction** attach **CN VI (abducens)** nearest the midline, with **CN VII (facial)** and **CN VIII (vestibulocochlear)** laterally.

**Medulla.** The ventral pyramids carry corticospinal fibres that decussate at the caudal medulla. **CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus)** and the cranial root of **CN XI (accessory)** exit through the lateral postolivary sulcus; **CN XII (hypoglossal)** exits in the preolivary sulcus between pyramid and olive. CN I and II are attached to the forebrain, not the brainstem.

blocks.title: Reticular formation
blocks.text: The reticular formation is a diffuse network of neurones running through the brainstem tegmentum. It has ascending projections that maintain arousal (the ascending reticular activating system, ARAS), descending projections that modulate motor and pain pathways, and groups of neurones that coordinate respiration, heart rate and blood pressure.

blocks.markdown: **Functions of the reticular formation.** (1) **Arousal:** the ARAS projects through the thalamus (and via the hypothalamus and basal forebrain) to the cortex. Damage to the upper pontine or midbrain tegmentum, or bilateral thalamic damage, causes **coma**; a unilateral cortical lesion does not. (2) **Cardiorespiratory control:** respiratory rhythm generating neurones in the medulla (the pre-Botzinger complex and respiratory groups) and pontine respiratory groups, and medullary vasomotor centres, which regulate heart rate and vascular tone via the autonomic nervous system. Medullary compromise therefore produces respiratory failure and cardiovascular collapse. (3) **Motor and pain modulation:** reticulospinal tracts influence tone and posture; descending pathways modulate pain.

blocks.title: A crossed syndrome of the midbrain
blocks.prompt: Explain the signs in the opening case: right CN III palsy (ptosis, eye down and out) with left hemiparesis.

steps.text: The right oculomotor nerve fascicle passes through the right midbrain on its way to exit in the interpeduncular fossa. A lesion there damages it, producing ipsilateral signs: ptosis and a down-and-out eye.
The right cerebral peduncle (basis) lies next to the fascicle and carries corticospinal fibres from the right motor cortex, which have not yet decussated (they cross at the caudal medulla).
Damage to these fibres therefore weakens the left arm and leg.

blocks.answer: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis localises to the right midbrain (Weber pattern).

blocks.title: Why crossed signs occur
blocks.text: Cranial nerve nuclei and fascicles act on the same side, whereas long tracts at the same level are either not yet crossed (corticospinal above the pyramidal decussation) or already crossed (spinothalamic). A single small lesion therefore damages an ipsilateral cranial nerve and a contralateral long tract, which is why crossed signs localise the lesion to the brainstem.

blocks.title: A crossed syndrome of the pons
blocks.prompt: A patient has an ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy and ipsilateral facial weakness, with contralateral limb weakness. Where is the lesion and why?

steps.text: The abducens nucleus and facial nerve fascicle lie in the caudal pontine tegmentum, so damage causes ipsilateral eye abduction failure and facial weakness.
The ventral pons (basis) contains corticospinal fibres that have not yet decussated.
A lesion involving the tegmentum and basis on one side therefore produces ipsilateral cranial nerve signs and contralateral hemiparesis.

blocks.answer: A lesion of the caudal pons on the side of the cranial nerve signs (a ventral pontine syndrome).

items: Midbrain lesions typically involve CN III and the cerebral peduncle.
Pontine lesions involve CN V, VI, VII or VIII with corticospinal fibres in the basis.
Medullary lesions involve CN IX, X, XII (and sensory trigeminal nucleus) with the corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus or spinothalamic tract.
Bilateral involvement of the reticular formation causes coma or respiratory failure.

points: The brainstem comprises midbrain (CN III, IV), pons (CN V, VI, VII, VIII) and medulla (CN IX, X, XI, XII); CN IV exits dorsally.
The reticular formation maintains arousal (ARAS), regulates respiration and cardiovascular function, and modulates motor and pain pathways.
Brainstem lesions cause crossed signs: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral long-tract signs.

questions.stem: Which group of cranial nerves attaches to the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction?

distractorRationale.a: III and IV attach to the midbrain and V at mid-pons.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: abducens, facial and vestibulocochlear nerves attach at the pontomedullary junction.
distractorRationale.c: IX, X and XI attach to the medulla.
distractorRationale.d: X and XI attach to the lateral medulla and XII to the preolivary sulcus.

questions.explanation: The abducens, facial and vestibulocochlear nerves attach where the pons meets the medulla. The trigeminal attaches laterally at mid-pons.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve exits the brainstem from its dorsal surface?

distractorRationale.a: The oculomotor nerve exits ventrally in the interpeduncular fossa.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the trochlear nerve exits dorsally below the inferior colliculus.
distractorRationale.c: The abducens exits ventrally at the pontomedullary junction.
distractorRationale.d: The hypoglossal exits ventrally in the preolivary sulcus.

questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to leave the dorsal surface of the brainstem, emerging just below the inferior colliculus.

questions.stem: Which set of cranial nerves is attached to the medulla oblongata?

distractorRationale.d: CN I and II attach to the forebrain.

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory (cranial root) and hypoglossal nerves are attached to the medulla.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a small haemorrhage that destroys the paramedian tegmentum of the upper pons and midbrain on both sides. She is unrousable with no eye opening to pain. Which structure's disruption best explains the unconsciousness?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the ARAS runs through the paramedian tegmentum and maintains cortical arousal.
distractorRationale.b: Pyramidal damage causes weakness, not coma.
distractorRationale.c: Medial lemniscus damage causes sensory loss.

questions.explanation: The ascending reticular activating system maintains arousal through projections to the thalamus and cortex. Bilateral damage to the upper pontine and midbrain tegmentum interrupts it and causes coma.

questions.stem: Raised pressure in the posterior fossa pushes the cerebellar tonsils downward through the foramen magnum and compresses the medulla. Which function is most immediately at risk?

options.text: Control of respiration and blood pressure

questions.correctOptionText: Control of respiration and blood pressure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: medullary reticular centres coordinate breathing and vasomotor tone.
distractorRationale.b: Visual perception is mediated by the occipital cortex.
distractorRationale.c: Voluntary facial movement is mediated by the motor cortex and facial nucleus in the pons.
distractorRationale.d: Hearing is not primarily mediated by the medulla.

questions.explanation: The medulla contains reticular neurones that generate respiratory rhythm and control cardiovascular tone. Compression threatens breathing and circulation, which is why tonsillar herniation can be fatal.

questions.stem: True or false: the reticular formation functions only as a sensory relay and has no role in motor control or autonomic function.
questions.explanation: The reticular formation has several roles: arousal, cardiorespiratory control and modulation of motor and pain pathways. It is not restricted to sensory relay.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a stroke. On protrusion his tongue deviates to the right, and he has weakness of the left arm and leg with loss of vibration sense in the left limbs. Where is the lesion?

distractorRationale.a: A left medial lesion would deviate the tongue to the left and weaken the right limbs.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the hypoglossal fascicle (ipsilateral tongue weakness), pyramid (contralateral hemiparesis) and medial lemniscus (contralateral vibration loss) lie in the medial medulla.
distractorRationale.c: The lateral medulla contains the spinal trigeminal tract, nucleus ambiguus and spinothalamic tract.
distractorRationale.d: A pontine lesion does not involve the hypoglossal fascicle.

questions.explanation: The hypoglossal fascicle is ipsilateral, so a weak right tongue deviates toward the right on protrusion. The pyramid and medial lemniscus are contralateral to the lesion, so left-sided weakness and vibration loss localise the lesion to the right medial medulla.

questions.stem: Why does a lesion in the midbrain or pons often produce ipsilateral cranial nerve signs together with contralateral limb weakness?

options.text: Cranial nerve nuclei project to the opposite side, while corticospinal fibres have already crossed
Cranial nerve fascicles act on the same side, while corticospinal fibres have not yet decussated at that level
The brainstem contains no long tracts
All cranial nerves decussate in the brainstem

questions.correctOptionText: Cranial nerve fascicles act on the same side, while corticospinal fibres have not yet decussated at that level

distractorRationale.a: Corticospinal fibres cross at the caudal medulla, not above.
distractorRationale.c: The brainstem carries all the long tracts.
distractorRationale.d: Most cranial nerves do not decussate within the brainstem.

questions.explanation: A cranial nerve nucleus or fascicle affects the same side of the head, while corticospinal fibres above the pyramidal decussation still serve the opposite side of the body. A single lesion thus produces crossed signs.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, right-sided facial numbness to pain, right Horner syndrome and loss of pain and temperature on the left body. Explain why the signs are crossed and name the likely level and side.
markingGuide: Spinal trigeminal tract/nucleus (ipsilateral face pain and temperature) is ipsilateral because trigeminal afferents have not yet crossed
Nucleus ambiguus (CN IX/X) gives hoarseness and dysphagia, ipsilateral
Descending sympathetic fibres give ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Spinothalamic tract has already crossed in the cord, so it carries contralateral body pain and temperature
questions.explanation: Structures acting on the same side of the head (trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, descending sympathetic fibres) are damaged on the right, whereas the spinothalamic fibres carrying left-body pain and temperature have already crossed. This lateral medullary pattern localises the lesion to the right medulla.

questions.stem: Describe the roles of the reticular formation in arousal and in cardiorespiratory control, and give one clinical consequence of damage to each.
markingGuide: Ascending reticular activating system projects via thalamus and other relays to the cortex to maintain wakefulness
Damage to the upper pontine or midbrain tegmentum (bilateral) causes coma
Medullary respiratory neurones generate respiratory rhythm, with pontine groups modulating it
Medullary vasomotor neurones regulate sympathetic outflow, heart rate and blood pressure
Medullary damage causes respiratory failure or circulatory collapse
questions.explanation: The reticular formation sustains arousal through ascending projections and regulates breathing and circulation through medullary neurones. Damage therefore causes coma in the rostral brainstem and respiratory or cardiovascular failure in the medulla.
